title: Virtue and Love
english: We must flee from the damages that come from laziness and avoid the poverty of virtues, rejecting the shame of being weak in good things.
Let us become men and let our heart be strengthened, as it is written.
For the Lord Jesus Christ gave us the examples of such virtue, saying that whoever does not take up their cross and follow him is not worthy of him.
I think it is necessary to confess that following Christ is better than all cowardice, but to be overwhelmed by fear is to make one's own burden.
Just as a newborn child can barely walk and cannot follow the swift young men, so it is impossible for one who looks only to their own weakness to follow in the footsteps of Christ.

Christ, who endured the cross, despising shame, and tasted the bitterness of death for us, although he was a passionless and immortal God, the Logos and the only-begotten Son of the Father, gave us an example and a pattern for imitation.
And on this very achievement, Paul also was emboldened to courage.

The disciple of Christ, who is also a soldier of Christ, hastens to crown himself with the advantages of virtue, having been rightly chosen as our commander due to his virtue, and who also, as commander, was rightly appointed by vote.
He was so devoted to Christ that he considered it nothing to suffer everything in order to become a genuine disciple of Christ.
For he says, 'What are you doing, weeping and troubling my heart? I am ready not only to be bound but also to die for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.' (Matthew 10:38)
He was such a person in faith, and in his own character, he would astonish anyone who learned about him.
He made fasting his weapon in the battles of the body, and like a proven soldier, he subjected the laws of the flesh to the good things of his mind.
He also overpowered the pleasure that tyrannized our limbs, as if he had taken one of his servants under his control, and subjected it to the will of the spirit.

But in order to benefit us as well, he again exhorts us, saying that he had often been in fasts, and 'I beat my body and enslave it, lest after preaching to others, I myself become disqualified.' (1 Corinthians 9:27)
He was mindful, as it seems, of the cry of his own Master.

The Lord teaches that whoever loosens one of the least commandments and teaches others to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven; whoever practices and teaches these commandments will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.
The Lord himself preached and practiced this, imposing fasting and abstinence on the flesh as a means to attain virtue.
The Lord's teachings go beyond self-control, guiding us towards the ultimate goal of love for one another.

This is emphasized by both the Lord and Paul, who writes to the Corinthians about the superiority of love over other gifts, stating that even the most extraordinary abilities are worthless without love.
The Lord's words, 'By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another,' highlight the importance of this virtue. (John 13:35)
The absence of love for God and for others makes even the most praiseworthy virtue appear unseemly and unattractive.
However, when love is present, it makes the glory of those who possess it most becoming.
If someone praises love as a great and wonderful thing, but does not define its nature or show how one can attain it, they will not speak well.
The sober disciple runs past nothing that is necessary, for they know that love is essential to true virtue.
The nature of love is described as patient, kind, and not envious or boastful; it does not behave unseemly, seek its own interests, or rejoice in iniquity.
Instead, it rejoices in the truth, bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things.
Love never fails, and it is the path to approval and the city above, whose craftsman and creator is God.
By following this path, we can arrive at the city above, coming in the chariot of the saints.

When we turn away from what is right and abandon our correct and straightforward judgment, we end up living a distorted life, which ultimately leads us to the depths of Hades, as the wise writer of Proverbs warns.

However, as rational human beings created in the image of our Creator, it is essential for us to be guided by the principles of love and to emulate the Lord, who teaches us to learn from Him and to cultivate gentleness and humility in our hearts.
In contrast to the savagery of wild beasts, which we should not imitate, even irrational animals and wild beasts are capable of living together and having common habits.
For instance, cattle and sheep associate with their own kind, and dogs, despite their natural instincts, can be tamed and learn to love each other like family members.

title: Repentance and Unity
english: Bears and lions, despite their ferocity, spare their own kind, but humans, who have been entrusted with leadership over all creation, often fail to recognize their own foolishness. This is because they mistakenly believe that courage is about being fearless, and that savagery is something to be proud of. They do not honor their common human nature, nor do they reverence the Creator who made them, nor do they consider anything else that contributes to sober reasoning. Instead, they boast shamelessly about things that should bring shame, so that Paul justly says: 'Their glory is in their shame' (Phil 3:19).

The prophet, in his wisdom, marvels at this state of affairs and asks, 'Did not one God create us? Is there not one Father of us all?' (Gen 2:24; Mal 2:10). He laments the fact that humans abandon their brothers and sisters, despite being of one origin. For just as there is one leader of the human race, Adam, and one God who created us, so too should we recognize our shared humanity and strive for unity, rather than division and strife. We should be bound together by natural ties of love and reject the unnatural madness that leads to fratricidal anger. This is the message that we bring to you, especially to those of you who inhabit the land of the Egyptians. Spiritual fathers should guide their children towards what is beneficial and a lawful civic life, rather than leaving them to be untaught and ignorant.

Frightful things are being reported to us, and it is said that some of you are daring to do the most shameful and difficult things. Young men, having become confident in their bodily strength, are misusing the needs of their youth and arming themselves with swords, and they are being taught to wield clubs more savagely than the law of their local custom allows.

They spend the prime of their life in unholy pursuits, either gathering pretexts for anger against their neighbors and attacking them irrationally, or loving the forgiveness of other people's money and not perceiving themselves to be entangling themselves in unbreakable snares, and subjecting themselves to death and bitter dangers. For it is written that transgressions hunt down a man, and each one is bound by the chains of their own sins (Prov 5:22).

But, my children, according to Paul, I testify to you with a loud voice, instructing the disorderly and guiding those who are still reckless in their youth, to stop such transgressions and to cease causing pain and provoking the King and Lord of all. You must cast away the murderous sword from your hand and the unjust desire for other people's things from your mind, and restrain your impulses towards each other, and calm your anger, and stop your unholy endeavors.

We must not look to Cain, the brother-killer, as an example. He was unfeeling and taught impiety through his violent actions. However, the Creator of all things spoke to him, saying, 'The voice of your brother's blood cries out to me from the earth' (Gen 4:10). This warning extends to all who would follow in his footsteps. Each person who dares to commit such atrocities should hear God's voice, which cries out no less today: 'The voice of your brother's blood cries out to me from the earth.' Just as it was told to him again, 'You will be groaning and trembling on the earth' (Gen 3:17), so too will God say to each of those who commit similar evils.

The one who transgresses the law is cowardly, and what word does not terrify him? Even a glance at himself is enough to make him shudder. For his conscience always falls within, convicted by the accusations of sin. On the other hand, the righteous one trusts like a lion and is a witness to every good work, fearless of every accusation. But the one who loves sin is weakened to cowardice. Therefore, let us heed the prophetic word, which says, 'Awake, you drunkards, from your wine…' (Amos 8:8).

All who indulge in excessive wine consumption are called to mourn, for the joy and cheer that once filled their lives have been taken away. The true word of experience is evident in our current situation, and it is a stark reminder of the consequences of our actions. The Egyptian farmers, who were once renowned for their fertile land, now have a tale of woe to tell. What kind of story can they share with us, and what kind of word can bring us joy and cheer in these desperate times? It seems that no one, regardless of their social status, has been spared from the devastating effects of the recently inflicted wrath. The prophet's words, which speak of the withering of the vine, the failure of the fig trees, and the drying up of the pomegranate, palm, and apple trees, are a poignant reminder of the desolation that has befallen us (Amos 8:23).

The good and merciful God, who is the giver of all good things, had provided us with a fruitful earth, but the inhabitants of the earth have been put to shame. The hills, which were once adorned with stately trees, now stand as a testament to the transience of human hopes and the fleeting nature of courage. The earth, which was once nourished by the blood of the righteous, has been drunk with human blood, and the sword of brotherly hatred has been lifted against each other. As a result, God has been justly angered, and we are left to mourn the loss of our joy and cheer.

The earth, which was once fruitful, has been fortified with fire, and the passions that were expected have been turned into lamentation, changing joy into sorrow. The prophet's words have come true, as we see the devastating effects of famine in our land. The food that was once abundant is now scarce, and the people are groaning with hunger, seeking bread.

The prophet Jeremiah lamented over the situation, saying that all the people are groaning, seeking bread (Jer 8:20), and that even the infants are suffering from thirst. The tongue of the suckling child has cleaved to its palate due to thirst, and there is no one to break bread for them. Those who once ate delicacies are now reduced to poverty in the streets. We have tried many things, but our efforts have been in vain, and we have provoked the Spirit of the Lord. Therefore, I will repent and reflect on the ancient things...
